exam.title: Statistics I - Exam B
exam.subtitle: Descriptive statistics, distributions and tests
exam.instructions: Complete all tasks thoroughly. Show your work. Permitted aids: non-programmable calculator, standard normal and t-distribution tables.

exercises.title: Summary statistics of a sample
exercises.description:
Given the measurements $4, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 15, 15$.
a) Compute mean and median.
b) Compute sample variance and standard deviation.
c) Determine the quartiles and the interquartile range.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Mean and median
$\sum x_i = 100$, $\bar x = \frac{100}{10} = 10$. Median ($n = 10$ even): average of the $5$th and $6$th values: $\frac{9 + 10}{2} = 9.5$.

Step 2: Part b): Variance
Squared deviations $(x_i - 10)^2$: $36, 9, 9, 4, 1, 0, 4, 9, 25, 25$, sum $122$. $s^2 = \frac{122}{9} \approx 13.56$, $s \approx 3.68$.

Step 3: Part c): Quartiles
Lower half $4,7,7,8,9$: $Q_1 = 7$. Upper half $10,12,13,15,15$: $Q_3 = 13$. $\mathrm{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1 = 6$.

Step 4: Check and interpretation
Sum of deviations: $-6 - 3 - 3 - 2 - 1 + 0 + 2 + 3 + 5 + 5 = 0$ ✓. Mean $>$ median: slightly left-skewed distribution (long tail downwards). Outlier rule: there are no values outside $[Q_1 - 1.5\,\mathrm{IQR},\ Q_3 + 1.5\,\mathrm{IQR}] = [-2, 22]$.

exercises.title: Binomial distribution in a multiple-choice test
exercises.description:
A test consists of $12$ questions with $4$ answer options each (exactly one correct). A student guesses every question. Let $X$ be the number of correct answers.
a) What distribution does $X$ have? Determine $E(X)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)$.
b) Determine $P(X = 3)$.
c) Determine $P(X \geq 1)$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Model
$12$ independent trials with $p = \frac14$: $X \sim B(12;\ 0.25)$. $E(X) = 12\cdot0.25 = 3$, $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 12\cdot0.25\cdot0.75 = 2.25$.

Step 2: Part b): Single probability
$P(X = 3) = \binom{12}{3}0.25^3\,0.75^9 = 220\cdot0.015625\cdot0.07508 \approx 0.2581$.

Step 3: Part c): Complement
$P(X \geq 1) = 1 - P(X = 0) = 1 - 0.75^{12} = 1 - 0.03168 \approx 0.9683$.

Step 4: Check
The expectation $3$ is also the most likely value; $P(X = 3) \approx 26\,\%$ is therefore plausible. Guessing hardly pays off: $P(X \geq 6) \approx 5.4\,\%$.

exercises.title: Standardisation and quantiles
exercises.description:
The filling weight of a package is normally distributed with $\mu = 500\ \mathrm g$ and $\sigma = 10\ \mathrm g$.
a) Determine $P(X < 485)$.
b) Determine $P(490 < X < 510)$.
c) What would $\mu$ have to be so that at most $1\,\%$ of the packages are below $485\ \mathrm g$?
solutionSteps:
Step 2: Part b)
$490$ and $510$ are $\mu \mp 1\sigma$: $P = 2\Phi(1) - 1 = 0.6827$.

Step 3: Part c): Condition
We need $\mu$ with $\Phi\left(\frac{485 - \mu}{10}\right) = 0.01$. From the table $\Phi(z) = 0.01$ for $z = -2.326$.

Step 4: Part c): Solving and check
$\frac{485 - \mu}{10} = -2.326 \Rightarrow \mu = 485 + 23.26 = 508.26\ \mathrm g$. Check: $z = \frac{485 - 508.26}{10} = -2.326$ ✓. The filling machine must therefore fill on average $\approx 508\ \mathrm g$ (consequence: avoid under-filling, but accept higher consumption).

exercises.title: Confidence interval for a proportion
exercises.description:
In a survey of $n = 400$ people, $240$ agree with a statement.
a) Determine the estimate $\hat p$.
b) Determine a $95\,\%$ confidence interval for the true proportion $p$.
c) How large would $n$ have to be so that the interval width is at most $0.04$?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Estimate
$\hat p = \frac{240}{400} = 0.6$.

Step 2: Part b): Interval
Standard error $\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.24}{400}} \approx 0.0245$. $\hat p \pm 1.96\cdot0.0245 = 0.6 \pm 0.048 \Rightarrow [0.552;\ 0.648]$.

Step 3: Part c): Sample size
Width $= 2\cdot1.96\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}} \leq 0.04 \iff \sqrt n \geq \frac{2\cdot1.96\cdot0.4899}{0.04} \approx 48.0 \iff n \geq 2305$. (With the worst case $\hat p = 0.5$ one would get $n \geq 2401$.)

Step 4: Check and interpretation
The width of the interval from b) is $0.096$; for $n = 2305$ we get $2\cdot1.96\sqrt{0.24/2305} \approx 0.040$ ✓. Quadrupling the sample size halves the width ($\propto 1/\sqrt n$).

exercises.title: z-test for the mean
exercises.description: A machine fills on average $\mu_0 = 100$ units, the standard deviation $\sigma = 12$ is known. A sample of $n = 36$ gives $\bar x = 104$. Test $H_0: \mu = 100$ against $H_1: \mu \neq 100$ at the $5\,\%$ level.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Test statistic
For known $\sigma$: $Z = \frac{\bar x - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n} = \frac{104 - 100}{12/6} = \frac42 = 2$. Under $H_0$, $Z \sim N(0,1)$.

Step 2: Decision via the critical value
Critical value (two-sided, $\alpha = 5\,\%$): $z_{0.975} = 1.96$. Since $|Z| = 2 > 1.96$, $H_0$ is **rejected**.

Step 3: Decision via the p-value
$p = 2(1 - \Phi(2)) = 2\cdot0.0228 = 0.0455 < 0.05$: same decision ✓.

Step 4: Interpretation and check
The deviation is significant at the $5\,\%$ level, but not at the $1\,\%$ level ($z_{0.995} = 2.576$). The $95\,\%$ confidence interval $104 \pm 1.96\cdot2 = [100.08;\ 107.92]$ does not contain $100$ — consistent with the rejection.
